passage: At the college investment club's Friday meeting, each member presented a practice portfolio, paper money only. Ojas went last. "I sold the solar company after it went up eight percent," Ojas said. "Locked in the win." "And the delivery startup?" asked Trisha, the club's faculty mentor. It was down forty percent since September. "I'm holding it. It'll come back." "What's your reason, apart from hoping?" Ojas looked at the screen for a long moment. "If I sell now, the loss becomes real." A few members nodded; they had done the same. Meanwhile the solar company had climbed another fifteen percent after Ojas sold it.

qa.q: How much was the delivery startup down since September?
qa.a: It was down forty percent since September.

qa.q: Why does Ojas hold on to the delivery startup?
qa.a: Selling would make the loss real and painful, so holding on feels safer, even without any reason beyond hope.

qa.q: What could Ojas try in the next round of the practice portfolio?
qa.a: Ojas could write down in advance why each holding was chosen and what would make it time to sell, then judge each one by that reason rather than by the pain of admitting a loss.

qa.q: How might the members who nodded feel hearing Ojas explain?
qa.a: They may feel a mix of relief and discomfort, recognising their own habit of holding losers and cashing in winners too early.

grounding: Shows a student holding a falling practice investment to avoid feeling the loss while selling a rising one too soon.

passage:
Dear Ayesha,
You asked how the café is doing. Honestly, badly. Eight months, and most days we don't cover the rent. Everyone says close it, but I can't. If I close, all the money and all those early mornings become a real loss, and right now it's still just a "slow phase". The funny thing is, my home cake orders were doing really well last year, and I stopped them the moment they made a small profit, because I was scared it wouldn't last. So I let go of the thing that worked and I'm clinging to the thing that doesn't. Writing this down, I can see how odd that sounds. Can we talk on Sunday? I think I need someone to ask me the hard questions.
Love,
Kavitha

qa.q: How long has the café been running?
qa.a: Eight months, and most days it doesn't cover the rent.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha keep calling it a "slow phase"?
qa.a: Calling it a slow phase avoids the pain of admitting the money and early mornings are lost, so the loss can stay unreal for now.

qa.q: What hard questions could Ayesha ask on Sunday?
qa.a: Ayesha could ask which business Kavitha would start today, what signs would show the café is really recovering, and whether the cake orders deserve another try.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel worried but hopeful, since the friend who wrote it is starting to see the pattern and is asking for help.

grounding: Shows a young adult keeping a failing café going to avoid facing the loss while having dropped a profitable side business too soon.

passage: Jeevan, you want the honest version? Fine. I'm Anirban, and for eighteen months I kept a game project alive that everyone, including me, knew was dying. Twelve downloads. Twelve! But shutting it down meant saying out loud that a year and a half was gone, and that hurt more than anything. Meanwhile I had a small design job for a local bakery that was actually paying and growing. The moment it made decent money I quit, because I was scared it would fall apart and I wanted to leave on a win. So I dropped the winner and kept feeding the loser. It took my sister asking, "Would you start this game today?" for me to finally let it go.

qa.q: How many downloads did the game have?
qa.a: The game had twelve downloads.

qa.q: Why did Anirban quit the paying design job?
qa.a: Anirban was scared it would fall apart and wanted to leave on a win, so locking in the good feeling felt safer than risking a loss later.

qa.q: What question finally helped Anirban, and why does it work?
qa.a: The sister's question, "Would you start this game today?", worked because it looks forward from now instead of back at the year and a half already spent.

qa.q: How might the bakery have been affected when Anirban quit?
qa.a: The bakery lost a designer whose work was helping it grow, probably without understanding why things ended just as they were going well.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding on to a failing project to avoid the pain of the loss while quitting a growing one too early.

passage: I'm Gopika, and I run the second-hand book stall at our college gate with Arnab. I can only tell you what I've seen, not what's in his head. In June he bought forty copies of an old-syllabus exam guide cheap, sure they'd sell. They didn't. The syllabus had changed. Every week I say, "Let's sell them to the raddi shop and use the shelf." Every week he says, "Wait. Someone will need them. If we sell now, we've lost the money." They're still there, gathering dust, taking half our shelf. Meanwhile, when the new engineering drawing books started flying off the table, Arnab sold the last five for a quick small profit the same afternoon. "Take the profit before it disappears," he said. We ran out by Monday, and ten students came asking. I don't get it. The good ones he can't let go of fast enough.

qa.q: How many copies of the old-syllabus exam guide did Arnab buy?
qa.a: He bought forty copies.

qa.q: Why might Arnab keep the old guides even though they don't sell?
qa.a: Selling them to the raddi shop would make the loss real and final. Waiting lets him avoid that pain, so holding on feels like the safer choice.

qa.q: What could Arnab ask himself to decide about the old guides more clearly?
qa.a: He could ask whether he would buy forty of those guides today for the space they take. If not, selling them and using the shelf for books that sell is the better choice from here.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel about sharing a stall with Arnab's habits?
qa.a: Gopika seems frustrated and puzzled, watching dead stock take half the shelf while the popular books run out too early.

grounding: A stall partner describes a student who holds on to unsellable stock to avoid facing the loss, while selling the best-selling books too soon.

passage:
January. With her first internship stipend, Usha, twenty-one, bought small amounts of two companies' shares. Within a month, one had risen 8% and one had fallen 12%. She sold the rising one straight away. "Lock it in before it drops," she told her friend Vishal. The falling one she kept. "It'll come back. If I sell, I've lost."
April. The one she sold had gone up another 20%. The one she held had fallen further. Usha stopped opening the app. She felt sick every time she thought of it, so she didn't think of it.
July. Vishal asked, "If you had this money in cash today, would you buy that company?" Usha was quiet. "No." "Then why are you holding it?" "Because selling means admitting I lost." She said it out loud and it sounded strange even to her. That night she wrote down what she'd learned before doing anything else.

qa.q: How much had the falling share dropped within the first month?
qa.a: It had fallen 12%.

qa.q: Why did Usha stop opening the app in April?
qa.a: Looking at the falling share made her feel sick, and avoiding it let her escape the pain of facing the loss. Not looking felt easier than deciding.

qa.q: What question from Vishal was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: "If you had this money in cash today, would you buy that company?" It made Usha judge the share from today, not from what she paid, and she saw she was holding it only to avoid admitting the loss.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt watching Usha across these months?
qa.a: Vishal was probably worried but patient, waiting for the right moment to ask one clear question instead of lecturing.

grounding: A young woman sells a rising share too soon and holds a falling one to avoid facing the loss, until a friend's question makes her see it.

passage:
Hi Francis,
You asked why I'm still doing the phone-cover printing thing. Honest answer: I can't bear to call it a loss. Eight months, the printer, the stock under my bed, and we've sold maybe forty covers. Every week I tell myself one more push and it'll turn. If I stop, then it's official that I wasted all that.
The funny part? The maths tutoring I started in January was actually working. Six kids, good feedback, parents asking for more slots. I quit it in March because I'd "had enough" and wanted time for the covers. I think I just wanted to lock in the win before it could go wrong.
Writing this down, it sounds backwards, doesn't it? Tell me honestly.
Pankaj

qa.q: How many covers has Pankaj sold in eight months?
qa.a: Maybe forty covers.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj keep going with the phone covers?
qa.a: Pankaj is afraid of the hurt of calling it a loss, so stopping feels like making the waste official, and hoping feels safer than admitting it.

qa.q: What would you advise Pankaj to think about?
qa.a: Judge each project by how it is likely to go from here, not by what is already spent, and look again at the tutoring that was working.

qa.q: How might Francis read this letter?
qa.a: Francis may feel glad Pankaj is being honest, and could gently agree that holding the failing project while dropping the working one sounds backwards.

grounding: A young adult keeps a failing side project going to avoid admitting the loss, after quitting a successful one early.

passage: Noor, you'll laugh, but I finally see what Disha does. Two years ago I started two things at college: the quiz club and the film society. The quiz club took off: sixty members, an inter-college win. And the moment it was doing well, I handed it to a junior. I told myself I'd done my part. I think I was scared it would fall and my win would go with it. The film society? Four people come, and one of them is me. The projector is broken. I've kept it going for two years, booking the room, making posters, because shutting it means saying out loud that it failed. Holding the bad one, letting go of the good one early. It's like I'm protecting myself from a feeling, not making a decision.

qa.q: How many members did the quiz club have?
qa.a: Sixty members.

qa.q: Why has Disha kept the film society going for two years?
qa.a: Disha dreads the hurt of admitting it failed, so booking rooms and making posters feels easier than saying it out loud.

qa.q: What question could help Disha decide about the film society?
qa.a: Whether Disha would start it today, with four members and a broken projector; if not, it may be time to close it and put energy where things work.

qa.q: What would change if Disha had kept leading the quiz club?
qa.a: The club might have grown further with Disha's energy, instead of that energy going into a society four people attend.

grounding: A student describes handing off a thriving club too soon while keeping a failing one alive to avoid admitting the loss.

passage:
Monday. Wasim's final-year project app still crashed on login, eight weeks in. Mridul, his teammate, suggested switching to the simple attendance tool they'd built in week two, the one that already worked. "We dropped that because it was too easy," Wasim said. "This one is ours now. We can't just throw eight weeks away."
Thursday. Another all-nighter. The login crashed again at 3 a.m. Wasim stared at the screen, eyes burning, and still said, "One more week and it'll work."
Saturday. Their guide looked at both. "The attendance tool works and the department actually needs it. The other one needs three more months." Wasim went quiet for a long time. Then he opened the old folder. "Okay. We finish the one that works." Mridul let out a breath he had been holding for weeks.

qa.q: How long had the team been working on the app?
qa.a: Eight weeks.

qa.q: Why did Wasim refuse to switch on Monday?
qa.a: He felt he couldn't bear to throw away eight weeks, so calling the app a loss hurt more than struggling on with it.

qa.q: What helped Wasim change course, and why?
qa.a: The guide comparing both projects plainly, which made Wasim judge what would work from now on rather than what had been spent.

qa.q: What was the week like for Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul was probably frustrated and tired, holding his breath for weeks while the working tool sat unused.

grounding: Over a week, a student clings to a failing project to avoid admitting the loss, after setting aside a working one too early.

passage: Shalini, you're keeping that failing club project going? Let me tell you about my canteen stall in college, when I was a young man of twenty-one in Nagpur. I sold two things: sandwiches and fresh lime juice. The juice sold out every day. The sandwiches, almost nobody bought. Every evening I threw bread away. But I couldn't stop making sandwiches. Stopping meant admitting I'd lost money on them, and that hurt too much. So I kept making them, hoping. Meanwhile, when the juice was selling well, I got nervous it would stop and cut it down to save lemons. Silly, no? I held on to the loser and let go of the winner. Only when my friend asked, "Omkar, if you started fresh, what would you sell?" did I see it. Juice. Only juice.

qa.q: What did Omkar sell at the canteen stall?
qa.a: Sandwiches and fresh lime juice.

qa.q: Why did young Omkar keep making sandwiches that didn't sell?
qa.a: Stopping meant facing the loss, which hurt too much, so holding on felt easier even as bread was wasted daily.

qa.q: At what point in the story did Omkar see clearly, and why?
qa.a: When his friend asked what he'd sell if starting fresh, it removed the pain of past losses from the choice, and the answer was clearly juice.

qa.q: How might Omkar's friend have felt watching the bread being thrown away?
qa.a: The friend probably felt puzzled and a bit frustrated, seeing the obvious answer before Omkar did.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young man, he kept a failing product to avoid admitting the loss while cutting back the one that worked.

passage: It was exam season, and Hrithik's laptop had broken, so he was editing videos on his phone at two in the morning. He ran a small video channel. His cooking shorts got thousands of views; his long travel series got almost none. Last month he'd stopped the cooking shorts. "They've peaked," he told his friend Seema. "Better quit while I'm ahead." But he kept pouring hours into the travel series, episode after episode, hoping it would take off. "I've done twelve already. If I stop now, all that work is gone." Seema looked at the numbers on his phone. "Hrithik, the cooking ones were still growing." He shook his head. He couldn't bear to call the travel series a loss. So he uploaded episode thirteen, at 2 a.m., with his exam in six hours.

qa.q: How many travel episodes had Hrithik already made?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik keep making the travel series?
qa.a: Calling it a loss would hurt, so he holds on, hoping it will succeed, even though it costs him sleep before an exam.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do to decide more clearly?
qa.a: He could ask which series he'd start if beginning today, look honestly at the numbers, and bring back the cooking shorts.

qa.q: How does Seema see Hrithik's choices?
qa.a: Seema sees the numbers clearly and seems concerned that he's dropping what works and holding on to what doesn't.

grounding: It shows a young adult who holds on to a failing project to avoid the pain of the loss while stopping the successful one too soon.

passage: At the Hyderabad college fest, Farida ran a stall selling handmade jewellery. On the first day, her beaded earrings sold out by noon. The big resin necklaces she'd spent weeks making sold none. On the second day, she made fewer earrings. "They've done well, I don't want to push my luck," she told her friend Devika. But she laid out every necklace in the front row. "I spent so much on the resin. I can't just give up on them." Devika watched customers walk past the necklaces and ask, "No more earrings?" By the evening, Farida had sold three pairs of earrings and still no necklaces. She sat on the stall stool, tired and a little hurt, arranging the necklaces again, as if a better row would change the result.

qa.q: What sold out by noon on the first day?
qa.a: Her beaded earrings.

qa.q: Why did Farida keep displaying the necklaces in the front row?
qa.a: She felt hurt at the thought of admitting the resin money was lost, so holding on felt better than accepting it.

qa.q: What could Farida try on the last day of the fest?
qa.a: She could make more of the earrings that customers want and move the necklaces aside, deciding from what sells now.

qa.q: How does Devika see the customers' reactions?
qa.a: Devika notices customers asking for earrings and ignoring necklaces, and seems to see the pattern clearly.

grounding: It shows a young adult who holds on to a failing product to avoid the pain of the loss while cutting back the winner too soon.

"Jaya, you're printing more tote bags? You still have forty unsold."

"They'll sell, Darshan. I just need the right post."

"You said that in August. And the earrings?"

"I stopped making those."

"The earrings sold out three times!"

"Exactly. I made enough from them. I didn't want to push my luck."

"So you stopped the thing that works, and you're doubling the thing that doesn't?"

"If I stop the totes now, the money I spent on printing is just gone. I'll have to admit it failed."

"It's already gone, Jaya. Whether you print more or not."

Jaya looked at the pile of bags in the corner of her hostel room. Her throat felt tight. "It hurts to say it out loud."

"I know. But what if you put that printing money into earrings instead?"

She picked up a pair from the last batch and turned it over in her fingers.

passage:
I'm Tanvir. In my second year of college, I spent eight months on a study-planner app that nobody used. Twelve downloads, and six were my friends.

Meanwhile, I'd made a small quiz website for my hostel as a joke. Three hundred people used it in a week. Afreen said, "Build that out!" I didn't. I shut it down after a month. I told myself I'd had my fun with it.

But the planner app? I kept adding features. Every time I thought of stopping, I felt a sting in my chest. Eight months, gone. So I kept going, month after month, hoping the numbers would turn.

Looking back, I let go of the winner too early because I was afraid of losing what it had given me. And I held the loser because stopping meant feeling the loss.

This year I restarted the quiz site. It's doing fine.

qa.q: How many downloads did Tanvir's study-planner app get?
qa.a: Twelve downloads, and six were my friends.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir keep working on the planner app?
qa.a: Tanvir felt a sting at the thought of eight months being gone, so continuing felt easier than accepting the loss.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do differently with the next project?
qa.a: Tanvir could set a clear check-in date and ask honestly whether to keep going, and grow the ideas that are working instead of ending them early.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Tanvir shut down the quiz site?
qa.a: Afreen may have felt disappointed and puzzled, since Afreen saw the quiz site's success and encouraged building it out.

grounding: A young adult keeps a failing app going to avoid the pain of loss, while shutting down a successful project too soon.

passage:
Mentor's note, college enterprise club

Jeevan's team ran a food stall at the fest this week. On day one, their lemonade sold out by noon; their momos barely sold at all.

On day two, Jeevan decided to stop making lemonade. "We've made enough on it," he said. He doubled the momos. When I asked why, he said, "We've spent so much on the steamer. If we stop the momos, all that is lost."

By evening they had forty plates of cold momos left.

I sat with the team afterwards. Jeevan looked miserable. I asked, "If you were starting today, which would you sell?" Nandini, his teammate, said "lemonade" before he could answer. He laughed a little.

We talked about how it's painful to admit a loss, so people hold on, and how people cash in on a win early to protect it.

They'll try again next month, lemonade first.

qa.q: How many plates of momos were left by evening?
qa.a: Forty plates of cold momos.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan keep making momos on day two?
qa.a: Jeevan felt that stopping would mean the money spent on the steamer was lost, and admitting that loss felt painful.

qa.q: What question did the mentor ask, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: The mentor asked which item they would sell if starting today, which helped the team look forward instead of protecting past spending.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt about Jeevan's choices during the fest?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt frustrated watching lemonade stop, which is why Nandini answered "lemonade" so quickly.

grounding: A mentor notes a student who keeps selling a losing item to avoid admitting the loss, while stopping a winner too early.

passage:
Lohri night, hostel room
Bonfire smoke still in my hair. Did the thrift-page accounts after dinner and felt sick.
The denim jackets sold in two days. I let the last three go cheap on Tuesday because I was scared the buyers would vanish and I'd lose the profit. Then four more people asked for them.
The leather-look boots: eleven pairs, bought in October, not one sold. Elizabeth said tonight, "Baljeet, put them on clearance, get something back, and buy more jackets." I said no. If I sell below what I paid, then it's real, then I've actually lost. If I wait, maybe January gets colder and someone wants them.
Elizabeth just raised an eyebrow and handed me a piece of peanut chikki from the bonfire.
Eleven boxes are still stacked under my bed. I keep not looking at them.

qa.q: How many pairs of boots are still unsold?
qa.a: Eleven pairs of the leather-look boots are still unsold.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet refuse to put the boots on clearance?
qa.a: Selling below cost would make the loss real, and that feels painful and a little shameful, so waiting and hoping feels safer to Baljeet than facing it.

qa.q: What could Baljeet try to decide more evenly?
qa.a: Baljeet could ask, as if starting fresh tonight, whether the space under the bed should hold boots or jackets, and talk it over with Elizabeth or someone experienced in running a small shop.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth seem to see the boots?
qa.a: Elizabeth sees them as stock stuck under the bed that could make room for the jackets people actually want, and seems patient but unconvinced by the waiting.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding on to stock that is not selling to avoid facing the loss, while letting the items that sold well go too soon.
